new_sovereign_parents.title: Ifá
new_sovereign_parents.description: The supreme epistemological system, sacred divinatory science, and cosmological wisdom matrix of Yorùbá civilization, encompassing the 256 Odù Ifá corpus revealed through Ọ̀rúnmìlà (Bara Àgbọnnìrègún).
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Primordial origin dating to the divine descent at Ilé-Ifẹ̀ and institutionalized across millennia as the intellectual, moral, and judicial foundation of Yorùbá governance and spiritual life.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: Ifá derives from the divine root 'fá' (to embrace, contain, and gather all knowledge). Represents pure intellectual discernment (Ìmọ̀), character ethics (Ìwà Rere), and cosmic balance (Àṣẹ).
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Operated via sixteen sacred palm nuts (Ikin Ifá), divining chain (Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀), carved wooden divination tray (Ọpọ́n Ifá), sacred yellow baphia camwood powder (Ìyẹ̀rosùn), and ivory or wooden tapper (Ìrókẹ́ Ifá).
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Consulted during all foundational rites of passage (naming, marriage, coronations, burials, war council, state policy). Custodians are initiated high priests (Babaláwo) and priestesses (Ìyanífá).
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ifá ló loni, Ifá ló l’ọ̀la, Ifá ló l’ọ̀tuntun ọjọ́ mọ́kàndínlógún.
Bí a bá bọ́jú, Ifá là ń kọ́kọ́ gbé yẹ̀ wò.
Ifá kì í puro, òtítọ́ inú ni Ifá ń gbé.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Venerated across Afro-Atlantic civilizations as Regla de Ocha/Lucumí/Ifá in Cuba, Candomblé Ketu in Brazil, and Orisha-Shango Baptist in Trinidad.
new_sovereign_parents.geographical_origin: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, Ọ̀yọ́, Èkìtì, Ìjẹ̀bú, Benin Republic.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Portray with supreme reverence; show Babaláwo dressed in pristine white or woven Aṣọ Òkè, casting Ọ̀pẹ̀lẹ̀ upon carved Ọpọ́n Ifá covered in gold-hued Ìyẹ̀rosùn.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Were Music
new_sovereign_parents.description: The historic Yorùbá Islamic musical genre and dawn awakening performance (Ajísààrì) during Ramadan, serving as the foundational stylistic and rhythmic precursor to modern Fújì music.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Flourished in late 19th and early 20th-century Lagos, Ìbàdàn, Ìjẹ̀bú, and Ọ̀yọ́ Muslim quarters as competitive youth street choirs awakening fasting believers, evolving into secular Fújì in the late 1960s under Alhaji Sikiru Ayinde Barrister.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'Ajísààrì' (those who awaken people for Sahur / dawn meal). Celebrates communal solidarity, vocal agility, rhythm, and moral social commentary.
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Acoustically driven by Sákárà frame drums, handheld agogo metal bells, sẹ̀kẹ̀rẹ̀ gourds, and improvisational call-and-response vocal counterpoints.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Performed in pre-dawn twilight through residential alleys, followed by competitive neighborhood exhibitions during Eid celebrations.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹni tó jí lówùúrọ̀ tó gbọ́ Were, á mọ̀ pé ọjọ́ tuntun ti dé.
Ajísààrì kì í sùn lójú agogo.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Heavily influenced West African Francophone and UK-diaspora Yorùbá community festivities and Afro-fusion percussion arrangements.
new_sovereign_parents.geographical_origin: Isale Eko (Lagos Island), Ìbàdàn, Ìjẹ̀bú-Òde, Ọ̀yọ́.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Capture dynamic lanterns swinging in early morning mist, young men singing vibrant polyphonic Yorùbá rhymes accompanied by sharp ringing agogo bells and sákárà drums.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Oogun
new_sovereign_parents.description: The ancestral estate, lineage landholding, compound residences, and familial inheritance (Ogún Ìdílé / Inú-Ilé) transmitted through patrilineal or cognatic descent in Yorùbá customary law.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Governed since antiquity by customary land tenure covenants, royal boundary markers, and council of lineage elders (Ẹbí / Baálé).
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ogún' (inheritance, patrimony, legacy). Anchored in the principle that land and lineage honor belong to three generations: those who came before, those living today, and those unborn.
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Demarcated by ancestral Peregun boundary trees (Dracaena arborea), earthen compound walls (Àgbàlá), and lineage shrine alcoves.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Distributed post-funeral rites by the senior lineage head (Mọgàjí / Baálé) under strict customary jurisprudence (Ìpín Ogún), ensuring orphan and widow maintenance.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọmọ tí kò kọ́ iṣẹ́, á ta ogún tí bàbá rẹ̀ fi sílẹ̀.
Ogún kì í jẹ́ kí ẹbí tú ká.
Inú ilé la ti ń kẹ́ṣẹ́ wálé.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Manifests in Afro-Brazilian Terreiro compound succession structures and Lucumí house-sanctuary spiritual family lineages.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Show lineage elders gathered under an ancient courtyard veranda (Ààfin or Agbo-Ilé) deliberating over ancestral boundary covenants.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Òògùn
new_sovereign_parents.description: The comprehensive Yorùbá pharmacopeia, traditional botanical medicine, therapeutic decoctions (Àgbọ), and protective spiritual formulations presided over by Ọ̀sanyìn.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Developed over thousands of years of botanical empirical trial and cosmological revelation across forest and savanna ecosystems.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: Rooted in the metaphysical and physiological unity of flora and human vital force (Ẹ̀mí). 'Ewé gbogbo kíkì òògùn' (All leaves are medicine).
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Prepared using clay herbal cooking pots (Ikòkò Àgbọ), stone grinders (Ọlọ), mortars (Odó), leaves, barks, roots, and consecrated talismans.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Administered by licensed herbal healers (Oníṣègùn) and priests (Adáhunṣe) for curing physiological afflictions, restoring prenatal vitality, and community protection.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ewé ń bẹ l’óko, òògùn ń bẹ l’óko.
Ọ̀sanyìn l’olórí ewé gbogbo.
Òògùn tó jẹ́, orúkọ ewé rẹ̀ la mọ̀.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Central to Afro-Cuban Osainista herbal lore and Brazilian Candomblé Osanyin leaf rituals (Sasanyin).
new_sovereign_parents.geographical_origin: Rainforests and savanna transitional belts of Yorùbáland.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Show fresh rainforest medicinal leaves with dewdrops, clay pots brewing steaming botanical infusions over wood embers.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Ẹ̀pà
new_sovereign_parents.description: The beloved legume, protein-rich staple, and commercial agricultural crop roasted with sea-sand, boiled in pods, or ground into culinary pastes and savory accompaniments across Yorùbáland.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Cultivated across Yorùbá savanna farmlands and central agrarian corridors; deeply paired with roasted plantain (Bọ̀lẹ̀) and cassava flakes (Gàrí) for centuries.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: Derived from agrarian Yorùbá botanical vocabulary denoting the ground-pod legume. Represents sustenance, abundance, and the joy of shared snacking (Faaji).
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Roasted in heated river sand inside wide shallow earthenware or cast-iron pans (Agbada-Aro) to ensure uniform caramelization without burning.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: A vital social street food, travel ration, and hospitable gift served with Gàrí, Ẹ̀kọ, or roasted corn (Àgbàdo Yíyan).
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹ̀pà kò lè fọ́ koro kò gbádùn.
Bí a bá ń jẹ ẹ̀pà, a kì í fọwọ́ rọ́ gágá.
Ẹ̀pà ńlá ló ń bẹ́ sọ́wọ́ ọlọ́rọ̀.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Known as peanut or goober (from Bantu nguba) across the African Diaspora; preserved in southern US soul food and Caribbean peanut stews.
new_sovereign_parents.geographical_origin: Ọ̀yọ́, Òkè-Ògùn, Ìbàdàn, Ìlọrin, Èkìtì farmlands.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Visually depict freshly roasted, golden-brown groundnuts emerging from dark hot river sand, served wrapped in clean green banana leaves beside steaming Bọ̀lẹ̀.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Àpáta
new_sovereign_parents.description: The monumental granite inselbergs, rocky sanctuary formations, sacred hills, and ancient ancestral refuges (such as Olúmo Rock in Abẹ́òkúta and Ìdánre Hills) anchoring Yorùbá territorial identity.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Served as impregnable citadel sanctuaries during the 19th-century Yorùbá civil wars, sheltering sovereign populations and giving birth to metropolitan city-states.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: Rooted in the permanence and immutability of the earth. 'Àpáta' embodies resilience, enduring sanctuary, and divine cosmic anchoring.
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Natural Precambrian granite monoliths, basalt outcroppings, carved hillside stairways, and natural stone caverns.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Venerated as protective geographic deities (Òrìṣà Òkè) where town founding rituals, annual civic covenants, and prayers for prosperity are enacted.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àpáta kì í jìnnìhìn fún òjò.
Àpáta ló ní ilẹ̀, kò sí ẹni tó lè yí i kúrò.
Bí ojú bá pọ́n wa, orí àpáta là ń sá pamọ́ sí.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Preserved in Afro-Caribbean folklore and Brazilian Quilombo geographic defense traditions as symbols of maroon resilience.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Wide cinematic drone panoramas sweeping across ancient majestic granite inselbergs rising out of tropical rainforest canopies.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Ẹlẹ́mù
new_sovereign_parents.description: The indigenous guild of master palm wine tappers and arborists skilled in climbing the royal oil palm (Ọ̀pẹ) and raffia palm to harvest fresh sap (Ẹ̀mù Ọ̀pẹ and Ògùrọ̀).
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Practiced across the forest belt since early agricultural settlement; regulated through customary forest guilds honoring Ògún (god of iron tools).
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ẹni tó ń mú ẹ̀mù' (he who harvests palm wine). Symbolizes courage, botanical expertise, heights mastery, and agrarian hospitality.
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Equipped with strong climbing ropes (Ìgbà), curved tapping gouge chisels, and hanging collecting gourds (Agbè).
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Provides essential sweet palm wine for marriage negotiations, naming ceremonies, royal court libations, and communal evening storytelling.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹlẹ́mù kì í pa ẹ̀mù rẹ̀ mọ́ lórí ọ̀pẹ.
Ẹlẹ́mù tó mọ ìgbà kò ní bọ́ lórí igi.
Ẹ̀mù tútù là ń ta fún olówó, ẹ̀mù kíkan la fi ń bọ Ògún.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Resonates with West African diaspora culinary cultures and Caribbean rum/punch fermentation rituals.
new_sovereign_parents.geographical_origin: Ondo, Osun, Ogun, Ekiti, and Lagos palm groves.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Show a seasoned tapper scaling a tall oil palm at daybreak using an authentic fibrous Ìgbà harness, lowering gourd filled with frothing white wine.

new_sovereign_parents.title: Ẹégún
new_sovereign_parents.description: The colloquial, living ritual embodiment of ancestral spirits (Ará Ọ̀run) walking among the living during annual festivals, mortuary rites, and civic blessings.
new_sovereign_parents.historical_timeline: Originating in classical Ọ̀yọ́-Ilé under the Aláàfin court and spread across every Yorùbá kingdom as the premier ancestral communion institution.
new_sovereign_parents.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'egungun' (ancestral bone/lineage foundation). The masquerade represents the living continuation of ancestral protection, moral law, and family continuity.
new_sovereign_parents.material_and_craftsmanship: Sumptuously costumed in layered brocades, velvet strips, carved wooden headdresses, mirror insets, and cowrie-studded aprons.
new_sovereign_parents.social_and_ritual_context: Summoned from the sacred ancestral grove (Ìgbàlẹ̀) by initiated priests (Alágbàá) to cleanse towns of epidemics and bless families.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹégún tó jó t’ó wọ̀gbálẹ̀, orúkọ rẹ̀ kò ní parẹ́.
Ẹni tí kò mọ ẹégún, á bẹ̀rù aṣọ rẹ̀.
Ará Ọ̀run kò ní gbà kí ayé bàjẹ́.
new_sovereign_parents.diaspora_connections: Actively preserved in Oyotunji African Village (USA) and Cuban Cabildo Egúngún funerary societies.
new_sovereign_parents.media_production_notes: Dynamic cinematic whirling of multi-colored fabric streamers accompanied by thundering Bàtá drums and singing women.

new_sub_variants.title: Àrọ̀kọ̀ Ẹfà (Love)
new_sub_variants.description: The classic Yorùbá semiotic token of love and mutual affection, constructed by stringing six cowrie shells (Ẹfà) face-to-face to express romantic yearning and union.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: Practiced across pre-colonial Yorùbá city-states as a discreet, dignified method of courtship between lovers.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ẹfà' (six cowries, derived from 'fà' meaning to attract or draw near). Encodes the proverb: 'Ẹfà ló ní kí o fà mọ́ mi' (Six cowries decree that you draw near to me).
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Six pristine white cowrie shells carefully perforated and strung along raffia thread or twisted cotton cord with shells facing each other.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Hand-delivered by a trusted emissary to a romantic interest; receiving an affirmative symbolic response seals courtship intentions.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ẹfà ló ní kí o fà mọ́ mi.
Àrọ̀kọ̀ tí a rán sí olólùfẹ́ kì í parọ́.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Survives symbolically in Afro-Cuban divination poetry (Ẹfà cowrie patterns in diloggún) as signs of love.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Macro close-up shot of six white cowries strung facing inward on natural braided fiber resting upon handwoven indigo cloth.

new_sub_variants.title: Àrọ̀kọ̀ Ẹ̀jọ́ (Dispute)
new_sub_variants.description: The formal semiotic notification of a dispute, pending litigation, or official summons to a palace tribunal, communicated by stringing eight cowries (Ẹ̀jọ́) facing outward.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: Served as pre-colonial writ of summons within the legal jurisprudence of Old Ọ̀yọ́ and Ògbóni judicial lodges.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ẹ̀jọ́' (eight cowries, a homophonic pun with 'ẹ̀jọ́' meaning dispute/lawsuit). Indicates that conflict must be resolved before the council of elders.
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Eight cowrie shells tied back-to-back facing away from each other along coarse dark cordage, sometimes tied with a knot.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Carried by royal court couriers (Ìkọ̀ Ọba) or Ògbóni emissaries to notify a party of legal claims against them.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àrọ̀kọ̀ ẹ̀jọ́ dé, kò sí àyè fún àwíwí.
Ẹ̀jọ́ kì í wọ ilé kí ó ma ní alárinà.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Referenced in historical accounts of 19th-century Yorùbá diplomatic letters preserved in colonial archives.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Show royal palace messenger handing a folded palm-leaf packet revealing eight outward-facing cowries to a village Baálé.

new_sub_variants.title: Ọ̀kọ̀ Ẹlẹ́ṣin
new_sub_variants.description: The long-shafted, balanced cavalry lance forged with a tempered leaf-shaped iron head and counterweight butt, utilized by Ọ̀yọ́ Empire mounted warriors (Ẹlẹ́ṣin) for tactical charges.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: Central to the imperial dominance of the Old Ọ̀yọ́ Empire across the savanna from the 16th through early 19th centuries.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ọ̀kọ̀' (spear/lance) and 'ẹlẹ́ṣin' (horseman/cavalryman). Embodying martial precision, velocity, and sovereign imperial expansion.
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Forged high-carbon bloomery iron blade affixed to a flexible, seasoned hardwood shaft with brass collar bands.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Consecrated before battle with libations to Ògún; wielded exclusively by aristocratic cavalry regiments under the command of Ọ̀yọ́ war lords.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọ̀kọ̀ ẹlẹ́ṣin kì í fò lójú ogun lásán.
Ẹlẹ́ṣin kì í fẹsẹ̀ tẹ ọ̀kọ̀ rẹ̀ mọ́lẹ̀.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Survives in Cuban Lucumí and Brazilian Candomblé iconography of Ògún and Ẹlẹ́gbára carrying martial spears.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Dramatic galloping cavalry charging across savanna grassland, lances held leveled at shoulder height with sunlight gleaming off polished iron tips.

new_sub_variants.title: Ọfà Ọdẹ
new_sub_variants.description: The specialized hunting arrow fitted with barbed iron tips and aerodynamic guinea-fowl feather fletching, crafted by indigenous guilds under the tutelage of Òṣọ́ọ̀sì.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: Predates firearm introduction by centuries; maintained by traditional hunters (Ọdẹ) as the quintessential woodland game implement.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'ọfà' (arrow) and 'ọdẹ' (hunter). Embodying stealth, patience, and non-wasteful harmony with the forest ecology.
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Straight reeds or split bamboo shafts fitted with hand-forged barbed iron bodkins and stabilized with three-vane feather fletching glued with tree resin.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Consecrated at hunter shrines with prayers to Òṣọ́ọ̀sì; carried in cylindrical leather quivers (Apó Ọfà) across shoulder straps.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Ọfà ọdẹ kì í lọ kí ó padà l’ọ́wọ́ òfo.
Ọdẹ tó mọ ọfà ta kì í ba igbó jẹ́.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Prominent in Cuban and Brazilian rites for Ochosi / Oxóssi (the divine hunter's bow and arrow emblem).
new_sub_variants.geographical_origin: Forest belts of Èkìtì, Òndó, Ọ̀yọ́, and Ìjẹ̀bú.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Silent hunter crouching in dense tropical forest, drawing a taut bamboo bow with a razor-sharp barbed iron arrow aimed through leaves.

new_sub_variants.title: Àdá Ìbílẹ̀
new_sub_variants.description: The traditional broad-tipped Yorùbá clearing cutlass forged by master blacksmiths (Àgbẹ̀dẹ), serving as the supreme implement for clearing bush and harvesting crops.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: A cornerstone of Yorùbá agrarian civilizational survival since the Iron Age, enabling forest clearing and yam cultivation across millennia.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'àdá' (machete) and 'ìbílẹ̀' (native/indigenous). Reflects the primordial pact with Ògún that raw iron transforms wilderness into civilization.
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Forged locally from tough bloomery or scrap iron, shaped with a front-heavy convex curved edge, and fitted with a carved hardwood handle secured with pitch.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Carried daily by farmers; sworn upon in traditional courts as an instrument of truth consecrated to Ògún.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Àdá kì í mọ orí olówó rẹ̀ kí ó ṣá a l’ọ́gbẹ́.
Iṣẹ́ àdá kọ́ l’ọkọ́ ń ṣe.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Represented throughout Caribbean Maroon and Afro-Cuban farm lore as the quintessential freedom machete of Ògún.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Sparks flying from a blacksmith's anvil as a glowing orange cutlass blade is hammered to sharp curvature, quenching in water with a hiss.

new_sub_variants.title: Idà Agẹmọ
new_sub_variants.description: The sacred curved brass-and-iron ceremonial broadsword carried by high priests (Olójà / Ọ̀rẹ́moje) during the ancient Agẹmọ masquerade festivals of the Ìjẹ̀bú kingdom.
new_sub_variants.historical_timeline: Originating in Ìjẹ̀bú antiquity as the royal and priestly emblem of unity among the sixteen Agẹmọ priest-kings.
new_sub_variants.etymology_and_philosophy: From 'idà' (sword) and 'Agẹmọ' (the chameleon-associated supreme deity of Ìjẹ̀bú). Symbolizes priestly sanctity, cosmic vigilance, and monarchical protection.
new_sub_variants.material_and_craftsmanship: Forged iron blade richly inlaid with repoussé brass animal totems (chameleons, crocodiles) and a cast brass figurative hilt.
new_sub_variants.social_and_ritual_context: Used in solemn ceremonial choreography to part the festival crowds, bless the Awùjalẹ̀ (King of Ìjẹ̀bú), and consecrate civic peace.
proverbs_and_oral_traditions: Idà Agẹmọ kì í sá lasan, àlàáfíà ló ń mú wá.
Agẹmọ tí kò l’ádé, idà rẹ̀ l’ọlá rẹ̀.
new_sub_variants.diaspora_connections: Preserved in Afro-Brazilian and Cuban Òrìṣà altar regalia for water and chameleon-linked divinities.
new_sub_variants.media_production_notes: Priestly procession through sacred palm mats with priest bearing the ornate brass-inlaid Idà Agẹmọ aloft under ceremonial parasols.
